title: (No AI) OpenAI president says it’s ‘building a family of devices’ for its AI chatbots
author: Stevie Bonifield
content:
![](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/gettyimages-2182154299.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0,0,100,100)

In an [interview with our friend Joanna Stern](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b_44Ra8msls) on [her YouTube channel](https://www.theverge.com/tech/874444/our-friend-joanna-stern-is-becoming-a-youtuber), OpenAI president Greg Brockman said the company is working on a "family of devices" for interacting with its AI models. However, Brockman didn't confirm [reports](https://www.theverge.com/ai-artificial-intelligence/965670/openai-chatgpt-ai-smart-speaker-hardware-device) that one of those devices is a smart speaker OpenAI's rumored to be launching in 2027, or earlier rumors that the device [might be a wearable](https://www.theverge.com/news/672533/jony-ive-sam-altman-ai-device-ipod-shuffle-ai-pin) like the Humane AI pin. He didn't give a release date, either, only saying that "you can expect them soon."

When asked about whether [Apple's lawsuit against OpenAI](https://www.theverge.com/tech/964350/apple-openai-lawsuit-trade-secrets) could impact the devices it's working on with former [Apple designer Jony Ive](https://www.theverge.com/news/827607/openai-hardware-prototype-chatgpt-jony-ive-sam-altman), Brockman said, "We are focused on o …

title: (No AI) Artists are lawyering up against AI slop, and some are even winning
author: Terrence O’Brien
content:
![a middle finger being at an AI sparkle](https://platform.theverge.com/wp-content/uploads/sites/2/2026/07/268669_The_artists_suing_AI_companies_AParkin.jpg?quality=90&strip=all&crop=0,0,100,100)

Artists whose work has been co-opted by AI are taking to court. | Image: Alex Parkin / The Verge

When _The Atlantic_ published a [searchable dataset](https://www.theatlantic.com/category/ai-watchdog/) of works used to train AI, Kirk Wallace Johnson, like a lot of artists, looked for his name out of curiosity. And, like a lot of artists, he found it. Essentially, his books, like _The Feather Thief_ and _The Fishermen and the Dragon -_ nonfiction tomes that he spent "five to six years researching, writing, and investigating" - had been pirated and fed to a chatbot. He says he felt a "cocktail" of emotions: "anger over the brazenness of the theft, worry over what this means for writers, and a healthy thirst for revenge on these massive corporations that have become galactically wealthy" using his …
